name: Computed-goto bytecode dispatch (versus switch dispatch)
listed_description: Toy bytecode virtual machine with seven opcodes, written once with a big switch and once with GCC/Clang computed goto dispatch table.
claim_text: The book says the computed goto VM is 23% faster than the single large switch; reported means about 1.41 ns versus 1.82 ns.
book_benchmark: Catch2 BENCHMARK_ADVANCED over a randomized bytecode array of 2^24 opcodes, switch_vm against computed_goto_vm; compiler, flags and CPU not stated in this chunk. Also notes CPython moved from switch to computed goto in 2008 and to a tail-call interpreter in 2025 (faster in some scenarios, slower in others).
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Implementing efficient algorithms

name: Tail-recursive Fibonacci with musttail (versus plain recursion)
listed_description: Iterative, naive recursive and tail-recursive factorial and Fibonacci compared; tail recursion forced with a clang::musttail style attribute macro.
claim_text: Book reports Fibonacci(32): naive recursion about 2,389,913 ns, tail-recursive about 6.94 ns, iterative about 6.74 ns.
book_benchmark: Google Benchmark, factorial 32768 and 65536 (all three about equal, 20 to 40 microseconds) and Fibonacci 16 and 32; compiler, flags and CPU not stated in this chunk.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Implementing efficient algorithms

name: C++ Containers Benchmark (vector, list, deque, plf::colony)
listed_description: Blog benchmark by Baptiste Wicht comparing std::vector, std::list, std::deque and plf::colony across usage scenarios; the book points to it for cache-friendliness results.
claim_text: The book calls plf::colony a bag-type container with great fast insertion and deletion of large data; no numbers quoted in the book.
book_benchmark: Not run by the book; external blog post. Source code location for the 2017 post not found (search showed only the 2012 predecessor under the author's articles repository).
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Writing cache-friendly code and Further reading

name: libcoro
listed_description: C++20 coroutine library with task, generator and ring_buffer types, async mutex and latch, thread pool, io scheduler and Linux networking.
book_benchmark: Book only uses it in a small thread-pool example filling a vector; no timing. Repo README shows single-machine ab and wrk numbers (about 110k and 326k requests per second on an i7-9750H) with no comparison.
guessed_baseline: std::async or raw thread pool, cppcoro
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Using coroutines and A practical example using libcoro

name: async_simple
listed_description: Alibaba Cloud asynchronous component library with C++20 stackless coroutines (Lazy) and stackful coroutines (Uthread), listed as a high-performance coroutine framework.
claim_text: Book lists it among high-performance coroutine frameworks; no numbers.
book_benchmark: Not benchmarked by the book. Repo README only points to a separate quantitative analysis report comparing Lazy and Uthread.
found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Using coroutines

name: cppcoro
listed_description: Library of C++ coroutine abstractions (task, generator, thread pool and more), mentioned as similar to libcoro.

name: COROIO

name: liburing4cpp

found_in: book: Software Architecture with C++, 2nd ed. (2025), ch. 13, Using coroutines (emerging or experimental libraries)
